title: Close the door the deploy left open
summary: Review an exposed deployment, choose least-privilege network rules, and keep secrets and images under control.

scenario.briefing: A contractor deployed the orders stack from a laptop. The compose file publishes PostgreSQL on every interface, runs the API as root, commits an API key in an environment block, and exposes the admin path without TLS. Review the deployment and choose the firewall rule set that restores the intended boundary.

objectives.description: Identify exposed services, secrets, and excessive privileges.
Explain private networking, secret custody, and image trust.

hints: A published port is reachable from outside the container network.
The database should only accept traffic from the application.
Secrets belong in a secret manager, not in a committed file.
Public traffic terminates TLS at the edge; admin and database access stay private.

misconceptions.description: Assuming a compose network keeps published ports private.
misconceptions.feedback: A published port binds on the host and can be reachable from outside. Do not publish the database, and bind admin access to a private network.

misconceptions.description: Trusting every host inside the VPC.
misconceptions.feedback: A flat VPC lets one compromised service reach the database. Scope the database rule to the application security group or subnet.

misconceptions.description: Treating VPN access as a replacement for authentication and authorization.
misconceptions.feedback: A VPN narrows the network path but does not identify the user or limit what they may do. Keep authentication and least privilege inside the boundary.

sections.title: Every exposed port is a decision
sections.body: Publishing a container port binds it on the host. A database published on 0.0.0.0 is reachable wherever the host is reachable. Keep data stores on a private network and let only the application connect.

sections.title: Secrets have a lifecycle
sections.body: An API key in a compose file, image layer, or git history is exposed even after deletion. Put secrets in a manager, inject them at runtime, scope them to the service, and rotate on suspicion.

sections.title: The image is part of the attack surface
sections.body: A root process, an unpinned base image, and a compiler left in the runtime image all widen the boundary. Use a non-root user, pin the base, scan the image, and keep build tools out of production.

steps.title: Review the deployment
steps.prompt: Select every supported finding and choose a verdict.
hints: Read every published port and bind address.
Check the container user and the environment block.
Look at how the admin path is reached.
Block the deployment: the database is public, the API is root, and a secret is committed.

artifact.title: compose.yaml
artifact.caption: Production stack submitted with the contractor handoff.
artifact.content:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    ports:
      - "0.0.0.0:5432:5432"
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: campus-prod-2024
  api:
    image: campus/api:latest
    user: root
    ports:
      - "443:3000"
    environment:
      STRIPE_KEY: sk_live_51H...
  admin:
    image: campus/admin:latest
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    depends_on:
      - db

findings.label: PostgreSQL is published on every host interface.
The API container runs as root.
A live payment key is committed in the compose environment.
The admin service is published without a private network or TLS boundary.
Binding port 443 proves TLS is terminated inside the API.

verdicts.label: Block until ports, user, secrets, and admin access are fixed

steps.explanation: The database is publicly reachable, the API runs as root, a live secret is in the file, and the admin service has no private boundary.

steps.title: Choose the network boundary
steps.prompt: Select the rule set that matches the intended traffic.
hints: The database only needs connections from the application.
Administrative shell access belongs on a private network.
Choose the rule set that allows 443 publicly, 5432 only from the app, and 22 only over VPN.

inputs.label: Internet client to the public web endpoint on 443
Administrator over VPN to SSH on 22

rules.label: Allow 443 from the internet, 5432 only from the app subnet, and 22 only from the VPN
Allow all traffic from the VPC and publish 5432 for remote support
Allow SSH from the internet with password login
Deny all traffic, including the public web endpoint

steps.explanation: Only the public web endpoint accepts internet traffic. The database accepts its application, and administration stays on the VPN.

steps.title: Keep the boundary after the fix
hints: A secret in git history remains exposed after deletion.
Build tools in production widen the attack surface.
Select private data paths, secret injection, image scanning, and re-authentication; reject VPN as authorization.

statements.label: Data stores should accept traffic only from the services that need them.
Secrets should be injected at runtime from a manager and rotated after exposure.
Images should be pinned, scanned, and run as a non-root user.
VPN access replaces per-user authentication and authorization.
Publishing port 443 guarantees the connection is encrypted end to end.

steps.explanation: Private paths, scoped secrets, hardened images, and real authentication keep the boundary after deployment.
